speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Conversation with John Houston Cushman took place in his home in Moscow on October 27th, 1977. The interviewer is Rachel Foxman. Well, I brought some questions I wanted specifically to ask you. Could you tell me something at all about your early education?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I grew up in a little town. There were nine of us in class, and we graduated in the class of 1909.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And where was this from?

speaker: John Cushman
words: In Gifford, Maine. It was near Bangor. And they had the winning basketball team for several years since the little school. It was amazing. And there were three girls, six boys and six boys went to college and the girls and one went to a finishing school. Married my cousin. And so. Did you two boys are the middle aged men now? I was valedictorian, which was not hard. well, they were only nine. as I think of it now, it seems quite ridiculous that that's, everyone should take the same percentage. We all had to take Latin for years and three years of ranch and the English and the management. And we all had the junior exhibition, which, in which we recited. I don't know what you got there. About seven minutes long. And then in the senior year, we we had a part and they graduate actors who had. And so we had to experience to do that. we had some rather good teachers too. They were generally from Bates College. Bates over Colby, Maine, Bowdoin. My three cousins went to Bowdoin.

speaker: John Cushman
words: So last year when I needed a hat specialist, I chose a man from Bowdoin over in Seattle. Doctor Michelle was born and in Switzerland, and he lives. He did live as a boy near Concord, Lexington. And then he got his his medical training at Columbia and came out to the Swedish hospital in Sierra Leone.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What year did you start college, your undergraduate work?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I went through Brown University.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What year did you enter?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I entered in 1909. In 1909, I graduated in 1913. Then I went up to Harvard for a year in 1914 and started teaching then at Syracuse University.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: While you were going to Harvard?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, no. I went there for five years and then came out here. I came here in 1919, about the time everyone was coming back from the war. It started to grow. I left Syracuse when they had about 5,000. We used to have 60 in a class in English, that's freshman English. We had three sections. You can imagine what that amounted to. While I was there in the English department, I did some plays for the English Club. Their activity was plays given out of doors. They had what they called the castle. They bought a rich man's home, which was built exactly like a medieval castle. It was quite a nice outdoor theater, too. I did a Barry play, The Admiral of Crichton. Then I did Prunella. Did you ever hear of that?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Never had.

speaker: John Cushman
words: The lead in that was Marguerite Clark. She was quite famous in movies later on. She did that play on the stage on Broadway. It has a musical accompaniment. I did a part in that, The Honorable Ernest Wooley. It was a goody like an Oscar Wilde play. Do you know the play?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: No, I don't.

speaker: John Cushman
words: It's an awfully attractive play. I think so, anyway. I have always taught Barry along with Shaw and Prunella and some of the later Victorians, I guess you'd call them, and Galsworthy, of course.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Are those the types of plays that were being put on when you were in school?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yeah, when I was at Harvard, yes. There was a wonderful stock company that played in Boston right near the public library and one of the railroad stations. You could get off there if you were coming, as I used to from Brown. It was near the original Massachusetts Tech before they moved across the Charles River, where they now are. It was a charming theater. I can't remember the man's name or the women's name because they were all quite well-known actors and they put on the Galsworthy plays and the Shaw plays. I got to be very familiar with all those. You wouldn't have them, of course, in a college town because they'd never put on so many. They did about one a week and they were excellent.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: You say you studied in the Workshop 47 at Harvard in the summer?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I didn't. I've done quite a lot with playwriting here. The pageant, you know, is the chief thing I did. I did that three times here and once in Boise. I recently turned in a copy of our production to the university, so they have it up there now to keep, I think.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What brought you up to Idaho?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I was going to go to New York and study plays. I taught five years and that's what I was going to do and think of acting, of course, not production particularly. I got this offer very late in the fall. It was while the head of my department was on vacation after summer school up at Pend Oreille Lake where he had a summer camp. I got hired at Pend Oreille and I thought that's where the university was. I was very surprised when I came in and found where it was. You get into Spokane at nine o'clock at night. I came from Syracuse, of course, and Chicago.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: You came by train?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes. I hadn't ever been farther than Niagara Falls, which is the next town you see. Well, two towns, Buffalo. At any rate, that evening I got on the little train that comes down here. It gets here at one o'clock in the morning. I left Syracuse when they were having their state fair. It's a very famous fair at Syracuse, the state fair. They were crowded and all that. I was glad to get out of town. I took my old boating housekeeper to see a play to celebrate my farewell. We went to see Denman Thompson in the old homestead. I thought it was quite an appropriate place for the purpose. Then when I landed here in Syracuse in Moscow, I found they were having the state fair here. I could hardly get a place to stay. It took me about a month before I got a room to live in for that year. That year I had a little heater that I had to get wood for and prepare. I never could decide whether I would chop my wood for the evening and have a nice warm going to bed. I usually get home from rehearsal late at night or else get it in the morning when I wanted to be comfortable at the start of the day before breakfast and use my kin being there. I couldn't do both. In the night I always slept with my window open. There's a great big family cat, a yellow one. He'd come in about three o'clock in the morning and he'd crawl down inside the covers down by my feet for an hour or two and get all warm. Then he'd crawl out again.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: So when you came to Moscow you boarded with the family?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I didn't board with them. I just ate wherever I could down on Main Street. I generally ate with some boys who were undergraduates. They weren't my students at all. We ate at cheap little hotels, I guess, mostly. It was good enough food. We ate occasionally at a cafeteria. I got acquainted with Miss Matthew. Have you heard anything? No, I'm afraid I haven't. Matthew, she was in France and she had graduated from Washington and had taught at Aberdeen the year before. She came over to Moscow and lived with a regent's widow. She was part of the social scene here. Now my work outside of the university, I started this in 1919. I came here in 1919 and I did plays through 1930.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Then I stopped. You must have done, it seems to me that that time period there were a lot of

speaker: John Cushman
words: different styles of drama being produced. Well, if so, I had nothing to go by except occasionally to go to Spokane to see a real show, but otherwise just movies. I was very lucky not to have many movies here, though. Mr. Kenworthy came the second year I was here. He and his wife were down very simply, little movies. The first show I did here, a long one, because we were doing lots of one-acters then. I used to do a series of one-acters about every month. That was pretty hard. You understand I taught a full course in English. I did that on the side.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: As well as being department head?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes. I was hired. No, I wasn't department head, but I did all the drama. Then another man, Mr. Chenoweth, you must have, he's one of later accounting. He came when I did and he took care of public speaking. He later became a philosopher. Then Baker Brownell, who went to Northwestern and became quite a famous professor, also of philosophy, he was teaching journalism. That's the way Dr. Mill and I had built his new department. We were all new. The only one of us who was a PhD wasn't really an English teacher at all. He turned out to be the poorest, but he had the most scholarly background. He came from Stanford. The department then started off very well. When I became head, when Dr. Mill died, we happened to have a department much like that. I think people enjoyed it because they were good teachers and because they were well-read men. It worked out very well. Of course, Idaho in those early years wasn't primarily interested in a scholarly education in English. They would be in ag or forestry or mining or something else. I so frequently had people say, well, I never heard of you. I'd say, well, were you in engineering or mining or something like that? Because they usually run as fast as they can to get away from English. I never had any trouble getting actors, though. The men always seemed to be willing to take the spots there. One year I had a bad time of it back east during the First World War. You see, that came along 1917. I didn't leave that until 1919. I had one play to do and I had about one man only that I could count on. I chose a little play that was based on a famous novel called Cranford. Have you heard of that, Cranford? It's really like a Jane Austen play. Lots of country ladies. It turned out to be a good little play anyway. For the war, there was hardly any undergraduates on the campus. We had a bad time of it with flu. I never got that then. It was not my problem. Now, out here, we did about two main plays plus the graduation play. The seniors always had a graduation play. That all was before my time. I always had an awful time. We had the play in the place in the auditorium. The next morning, Sunday morning, was the commencement. They had to clear out everything on the stage and have it ready, fixed for the morning. I tried to get a play that wasn't too long. Some of the best plays we did were those commencement plays. I did one called Pygmalion. It was awfully well done. My hero lead was a fellow who became a famous chemistry man, a goody like Malcolm Renfrew. He settled in California, in Los Angeles. He was trained north at one of those schools in Chicago. He did that play. His sister's name was Verna Johanneson. Do you have her name? She was connected with the home economics school there. Then went over to Wyoming. She was married as a girl about 35. Her husband died within a year. It was rather tragic. She had a happy life. She was a home ec. all her life, I guess. Now, the first play I did here you'll be interested in. That spring sometime, while I was at Brown, I had to be going through Boston. I lived in Maine, so I always went through Boston. I'd stop off and see a play. This one was Billie Burke. You've heard of her, Andrew?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Sure have.

speaker: John Cushman
words: She was very famous then. She was in this play called The Amazons by Arthur Penaro. It's about a mother, a lord and lady who live in England. They bring their three girls up like boys because the father was so disappointed not to have boys. They also tried to keep all men away from them. The comedians were all men. We did this out in Derry. We did it also in Lewiston. I started that quite early, this spring out of town. We played in Kellogg and Wallace and the ones up where the lakes are. Coeur d'Alene? Coeur d'Alene and farther up. I remember having to hold a door up, I know, when people made firm exits. We couldn't nail together at the last moment.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Were the plays pretty well received?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh yes, they were. This first play, which I entertained the hero for just a short time ago, he came back for his 55th anniversary from Boise. He came here to this apartment and he now lives in the same type. He was a lawyer, trained as a lawyer. The law dean never liked me very much because I distracted some of his students. Another one of them became a judge and he was one of my best actors. I had an awful time with these lawyers because they were trained in high school so rigidly that they couldn't relax and take different parts. They could make their voice sound so they could be heard. That's something. Well, this play, The Amazons, is really still, I think, a pretty good high school play to be. At any rate, Bill Hager did it charmingly and amusingly. I did that for my first show. I, of course, had it much easier doing plays because they didn't have so many movies, you see. They hadn't seen the plays that I chose. And there were several jaunty writers then. I nearly always chose Broadway plays and Shakespeare. Some of my best, of course, were Romeo and Juliet and Twelfth Night. We used to take those to Spokane because in the spring the teachers all met up there and they hoped to get their first jobs at the meeting. And so the president of the university would generally get us an invitation to appear in the Lewis and Clark High School. And so I took all my scenery for Romeo and Juliet, which is staircases and all that, that would be modern. And we took the local drayman to tug it up there for us. We had modern lights to use, you know, spotlighting. And that's what makes those things work.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: When you first came here, I suppose you did some performing in the U-Hud?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, yes. That's where we finally went. I had that for my offers too. I occasionally had some of my regular English courses. I know the novel course was always over there. They just came into my office and sat around in a circle. Lola Clyde was in that class. And the first year I was here, I had non-dramatic literature for English, an advanced English course. I saw one of the girls last summer, and she's in her 70s somewhere. And of course, she doesn't look the same at all. But I was so amused that I was hired to do the plays and have the non-Shakespearean plays. And Dr. Miller, who was my chief, also had Dr. Kittredge from Harvard in Shakespeare. So naturally, he wanted to do that and did do it for several years before I came to it.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: When would you use the U-Hud facility instead of using the auditorium?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, that never happened. I always used the auditorium.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Always used the auditorium?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, I was in a scrap with the music head because he wanted to use it always. I had to go to the president sometimes to get my share. I used to help him, too. I did pinafore. I coached pinafore for him, and he did the singing. And I have occasionally done things like that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Was the U-Hud not big enough for you to use?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, no.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Is that why?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, no. We would try it for things that we wanted to do. We used masks, for instance, for some of our plays, our one actors. We tried usually those things on our one actors. But we found that the masks closed in their voices too much. We didn't know how to make them exactly. One of the girls liked the idea of making masks, and so she did them for us. And we used that kind of help how we could.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What kind of play would you use that mask for?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, it was something connected with the desert down around New Mexico. I can't remember. They must have been Spanish or Mexican.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: So it was rather experimental?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Is that what mostly it was used for?

speaker: John Cushman
words: That's what we did the U-Hud for, a lot of it. Not always. Sometimes it was just a pass, and some of the actors were lazy boys, and they hated to memorize their parts and so forth. But then I could tell from the work they did in my place if I could depend on them for a long part.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Well, I don't know if I understand. When you first came here, was there a department of drama?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, there wasn't. I developed that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And when did you develop the drama department?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I couldn't tell you. I developed also the club that they wanted to have. And so we had a little pen that looked like a drop curtain, and we called the club the curtain.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Curtain club.

speaker: John Cushman
words: The curtain club. And that was about the time Miss Collette was a student. You see, I had her. When she came here first, she was tried out, and she went off to college. And then she came back after two or three years as an assistant in the department. Well, she came back, really, just as I had, to teach full-time in English. And then she took over that work gradually in drama.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: When you would do plays, would you be the one that would be designing the sets as well?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I did all that, yes. I had some very good help. I had the college carpenter. He was a wonderful carpenter, and he'd do these broad staircases. They were far too heavy. When I was in Syracuse, I did a play for the Drama League, which was a national organization, and did it downtown in one of the big city theaters. And I did a play that one of the local janitors recognized. He said, well, I know what this is. I used to do this in New York. I worked on the play in New York, and it was Alice in the Fire, and that was by Barry. And the reason was that in the first act, a young girl had decorated the apartment, and she tried different kinds of wallpaper. So there's all kinds of wallpaper. Everything was crazy about the set. So of course, a fellow who was setting the stage would recognize that. And in Romeo and Juliet, Mercutio died, of course, about the middle of the play. And then he became the stage manager. So he had a little skullcap on his head. He was directing the evening of the drops overhead when the curtain accidentally slid open, seeing Mercutio, the dead Mercutio, doing the things with his wings. So he felt chagrined. I've been a reader ever since. I did a great deal of that, too. I had done it before I came here. And I did a group of plays in the Episcopal Guild Hall, where they had a little stage. And we used to read the plays with a book in our hand, and we'd act them out. I found myself one evening doing a part in a cot with a dignified lady of the land here, who used to be here and was doing one of the parts. So she was reading out of her book in the bed. We used to do a play every two weeks. We'd have four rehearsals. We didn't memorize them, you see. They worked very well. I did that four years. And that's beside the plays I did on the campus.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: How long would it take you to do a play that you do on the campus, a full-length play?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, I suppose six weeks.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Six weeks?

speaker: John Cushman
words: For the one-act plays.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And how long for the full-length plays?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, not much longer, but we'd have more rehearsals. We had them sometimes in the afternoon. It'd be so cold that I could hardly sit in my car after a rehearsal. It'd be that long.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And you were teaching drama classes at that time, too, as well?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, yes. We organized introductory courses, for instance, and advanced courses. I did advanced writing, too. In my early years, it was very interesting. I always enjoyed it. I think my best course was grade books, and I started that in 25. Professor—President Dale asked me to do it for the business school, so we'd have about 150. And I had three Episcopalian daughters who would read my quizzes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Sounded like they spread you pretty thin when you started teaching.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, I did a lot of that. After I stopped being head of the department, I had about five courses. I taught until I was 70. You see, most of them stopped at 65. But it didn't seem to cause me any trouble, and I enjoyed it a lot.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: You know, I have one more question about theater right now. And it seems to me that they don't do as much Shakespeare now on the campus. It sounds like when you were there, they did a lot more. Probably not.

speaker: John Cushman
words: They—what was style was barbed hair, and I protested it for acting, you see. And they quoted it in one of the arguments. I noticed what I had to say about barbed hair.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What was it that you had to say?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, that I didn't approve of it, because I didn't want to have to work with barbed hair. I wanted them to have the long hair as you have. And we could do all kinds of things with it, you see. Of course, they have gorgeous hair for Shakespeare as far as the men go. They have really beautiful hair, some of them.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Do you think that people could understand Shakespeare better, though, than they do?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I had Mr. Jennings, and he translated Shakespeare's plays. And even Dr. Miller, my superior, he recognized that we had translated—everybody didn't realize that he could understand it all. And he translated. And he did Romeo and Juliet, you know, in the movies, too. And he was used to that. We had some very interesting people.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Mr. Jennings sounds like he was a very interesting man.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, he was a fine, fine writer. Even Professor Baker found him a fine writer. He did two or three plays for him.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Can you tell me at all what that pageant was like, Light on the Mountain?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, yes, it was pretty good. And we competed that year, the first time, with Walla Walla. They did theirs more artificially. Their staging was built with wood. The mountains were built with wood somehow.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What was the competition?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, that, you see, we did it naturally on the athletic field. And so we'd look up on the top of the hill there, the arboretum, and Abe Goff was up there on a wooden horse, and he showed only when it turned the light on. We had some trouble with our lighting at first, but I finally got that better. Professor Johnson of electrical engineering, he was the head of that. He did that for me. And then we had an electrician, Ralph, what is his last name? I can't think of his last name. He's not living. But he was on the campus here, and he did all of that for me.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Who came up with the idea to do this pageant?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Dr. Miller, I think, because he had taught it some, and he had studied it in the East. Pageantry had been well known, of course, and was a way of getting your early English plays, you know. And so I think he started it. I didn't.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And Talbot Jennings wrote the play for him?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, he worked with me on that, of course. And also Professor Brossman, who was the American history man. But we had a great big committee. We had the dean of women, and we had the president of the university, and all sorts of people.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: How many people did you have in the production?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, gracious, I couldn't say. I had to have a lot of help. And some of the pageants, some of the later ones, Miss Collette and somebody who did Mr. Chavez's work, he would be doing it. I didn't finish talking to you, did I, about the assistance I had. One of my actresses, Hester Bren, Harry Bren is his name, and he was a painter. He was painting his way through college. He painted houses and things like that. And so he used to paint all the scenery for me, and that was kind of him. I would have been no good at it. Now that summer when I worked at Harvard, they sent me to getting doorknobs and things like that, and I was no good at all at that. I didn't happen to have done that kind of thing as a boy. Some of them here have done all that. And I would advise a person not to take so much French or Latin as I took. I could have taught those as well as my English if I had gone about it. At Brown, we didn't have any major work. They told us what we had to do, and that we did. And we had practically no choice. And it still does good work.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Well, when you say that you had the competition with Walla Walla, was it like a regional?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I mean to say in the area. I mean in the Northwest.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Oh, for people going to see the plays?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Or was it like a state level competition?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, they compared their show with ours. They have had one recently, I understand, two years ago that was very good.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Trails West? Yes.

speaker: John Cushman
words: I didn't see that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And did they do Light of the Mountain every year?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, they didn't. You see, I did it only about three times in all the years I was here. Governor McConnell was present. He was a little newsboy in the story. And so he was in it. And then when we did it in Boise, the law firm, I can't think of their name, but they did it. They were young boys then. Something begins with H. Funny, I can't think. I didn't know anything about the history, you see. But Mr. Jennings did. He was an Idaho boy. And so I depended on him. We had a bell. So we had a chapel. And we had a priest. That's one thing. We had a starting in with a group of football men, which I used for Indians. And then we got costumes by getting the Nez Perce Indians up here. And they each brought a costume. And so these boys wore those. And they looked like Indians because they were big and husky. But by the time we got through dancing them, they went through an Indian dance. And then they had a great long Ear of Arthur-like poem to recite, chanting around the campfires. That's the way we started, with the campfire. And we chanted all about Sacagawea being swiped by some other tribe of Indians. And then she appeared on the hilltop with Lewis and Clark leading them to Portland and so forth. And we introduced her by that, chanting around the campfire. But they found they couldn't do their regular football tactics and then have any breath left to recite. But we got wonderful effects. One of the girls danced, who sang soprano. She came. We put her in with the covered wagons. And they were way down the other end. And you looked way down and saw them coming into a circle to protect themselves from the attacks from Indians. And she sang soprano, Home Sweet Home, which was lovely. On the do-do, you know, you can get quite nice effects. And then we called the end, which we planned, the Dance of the Barren Wastes. The Dance of the Barren Wastes. And so they came down out of the hills with capes on, long capes that come to the ground. And they were the color of sagebrush. And they scooched down. And there are other in blues and greens and whites of the water come dancing down among them all. And then they'd rise up in the colors of yellow and peach color and all the fruits and apples and things like that. And then the dancing of those two colors, that is the waters and the fruits. And that was the final scene of the pageant.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: The book Beacon for Mountain and Plain says the scene where there was a lot of square dancing was a great favorite. Yes.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, Mrs. Bren made her hit in that. She was one of the partners that you got from some country farm to go with a horse and buggy across sagebrush and then dance all night. And as they did, you know, and then that's the way we gathered them, horses from the country here. We had an awful lot of horses and they were taken care of by the Ag Department. And we had the horses, we had Chief Joseph practically tied on his horse because he didn't know a horse from an alligator. And he had a white horse. He was like a circus. And he had that lovely speech, where the sun now stands, we'll fight no more forever. And he did it beautifully. I think he was a Jewish lad and his features were right for the part. He probably looked more romantic or at least heroic than Chief Joseph himself. It was very well built. And there was one fellow from up north here, who was kind of a star man, we called him. And he would read the stars and prophesy, I suppose, and kind of preach and so forth.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I understand one scene took place out of the memory of Dean French's childhood.

speaker: John Cushman
words: That I don't remember. I don't know as I know that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Something from, was quoted from Beacon for Mountain and Plain, I believe it was the Idaho City scene.

speaker: John Cushman
words: I see. I read that, of course. But I wouldn't know some of those things, I suppose. Though I knew the Dean very well.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: The pageant sounds like it was grand. Do you think they could do it nowadays?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, they don't have any place to do it.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: No, that's true.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Usually they filled all that back up.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: With buildings.

speaker: John Cushman
words: I don't know why they do it. I wish they would. I'd love to see it.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Yeah. It's interesting to hear about it.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I've heard a great deal about George Miller Morey, was that his name?

speaker: John Cushman
words: George Morey Miller, yes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: George Morey Miller. Yes. He was your dean?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes. He hired me, yes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It seems to me that he's quite well known and that he was pretty well respected.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, he looked like a farmer, exactly. Overalls. He liked to make farms and he dressed the part. He loved to go hunting and so he would look that way.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Was he an Idaho boy originally?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, no. He was from Indiana. He had come just two years before I did. He was much older. He's been gone now about, I wonder how many years. His son has died, too.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did you know anything at all about something called the Hume fights, named after Dean Hume? Yes.

speaker: John Cushman
words: I don't know how much of a fight there was, but he was a brilliant teacher. And he went to Stanford. He was my dean for the first year I was here, but he wasn't here. He was on leave. I don't know if Eric lived here in my time since 1919. But I don't know what the fight would be about.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Well, as I understand it, there was a big dispute between freshmen and sophomores.

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I didn't know that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: So the dean would just simply have them all line up as teams and play like a rough football game.

speaker: John Cushman
words: I never heard that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I wondered if that had been a tradition when you were here.

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, no, it hadn't been.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I understand Dean French was a great influence on this.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, I think she was about the strongest dean in the Northwest, no matter what the school was.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Why is that?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I don't know except for her personality. She was an Irish girl and she seemed very dignified. She said she helped Julia Milo put on her cap and gown for an honorary degree that they each got in Washington. And she could have done it, certainly. I used to see Julia Milo when I was in college with her husband, Southern and Milo. And they would do all the late Shakespeare plays and all. I was very lucky, as many, of course, were who went to Eastern schools, particularly, and had the money to go see the plays. And I think the luckiest one I saw was Alan Nizimov doing The Doll's House and Heather Gabler and all those. She'd do one after another. She just loved me. Just loved me. She learned English, too. She talked to me in Russian at first. Do you read those books? Like Cheryl Crawford. Cheryl Crawford is a producer and she worked with Alan Nizimov and that other one that has a repertory company in New York. They did several plays. That's in her old age, really. When I saw her first, of course, she was much younger. That's the only thing I regretted, not living out here, which I enjoyed, but being back east to see the plays. So I always kept up the theater arts as one. And the New Yorker nowadays that tells about the plays.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It seems like it was the 20s and the 30s was an outstanding time.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I'm surprised because when I look back at some of those plays, Mr. Tometz, who was here for his 55th anniversary this year, was in a play called Clarence. Do you know that? It's by Booth Tarkinger. When you read those plays in the 20s, they seem awfully simple. I can't imagine why I like them. I go to see all those plays that they have over here at the Student Union where they have a dinner, you know, and then they have a play. And most of those are about that period. And I've enjoyed all of those. I think I studied also the pageantry because I studied with Professor Baker. He had a course in all of English lit from the start. And so if you study those early plays, and then you know pretty well what pageantry is all about. Dr. Miller also studied with an English professor who knew a lot about English ballads, and that comes into it too. And so it was natural if you went to Harvard to be in on that and that kind of dramatic literature.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It seems like Professor Baker was probably one of the most outstanding men of that time for to study drama.

speaker: John Cushman
words: In the world, yes. He was.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Is there any reason why in particular that he was?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I don't know because what he was famous for in my time in college was debate. And he wrote a book on debate. And but this drama business came into his interest later.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Was it because he was the first one teaching theory in Christchurch? I think so.

speaker: John Cushman
words: They had two or three other ones in the country, but there's one in Iowa. And there's, I think, one in Michigan.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: University of Michigan? Yes. And was the other one Grinnell in Iowa, possibly? Or University of Iowa?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, it's the University of Iowa. The one I'm thinking about. And of course, they had one in Pittsburgh.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: But Baker seems to be the one that... Yes. When you talk about the plays that were coming out of the 20s, you talk about Thomas Wolfe.

speaker: John Cushman
words: His lectures were kind of dull because I think they were a little dusty. He seemed to have had them a long time and didn't keep up with them the way one could. We didn't have anyone at Brown quite like him. We had one man, however, who did the plays. And he was a charming person. And he gave dramatic readings that were very attractive.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: When you were here, did you do any of the Eugene O'Neill plays at all?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, of course, I taught a course in drama always, modern drama. And that included the O'Neill plays. Some of these have been written since I stopped teaching. Long Day's Journey into Night. There's some of those I knew, however, but I never incorporated them in the course.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Well, how did people out here in the West take to all this drama knowledge that you had?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I don't know. I tell you, when I taught great books, I taught the Bible. And some of my most enthusiastic people were the Mormon bishop and his wife. So I got by with them. And I never had known anything about them. At Syracuse, where I taught, it was a Methodist school. Not that I went to the Methodist church. I had an awful lot of Methodist ministers in my freshman English who were learning English. I hope they learned it. I'd have fellows 30 or 40 or 50, and women too at that time.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: When you were at Harvard, were there women allowed in the school?

speaker: John Cushman
words: There were over a night, yes, but we didn't see them very often. The women who worked in the library at Harvard had to wear long sleeves. They wouldn't permit them to do anything so daring. They had to have short sleeves. And I talked with one girl who worked in the library. We were quite amused at how strict they were.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Must have made it difficult for them in the summer when it got so warm.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, yes. Long sleeves.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I would think there'd be a lot of difference in approach between what was being taught in the East and what was being taught in the West.

speaker: John Cushman
words: I think there is. Now my oldest granddaughter is 13 and she started German this year. And I told her parents I regret it. I took German too, but I thought French was so much better. And in New England, you find French used a lot more than German. Of course, if you had the same kind of training I did, you probably would get both.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did you find much difference in the discipline between the students that you had in the East and the ones that you had in the West?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I'll tell you what it's like for examination, final examination. We'd go to the chapel when it was time for our exam. And I would be looking for a certain course I was taking. And it would say, instead of blue book, it might say pink book or red book or yellow book or some other color. And then you'd go and sit down at one of those books. And they had people pacing up and down constantly. And there's no one there who was in my class. So I couldn't have possibly cheated. But they had this pacing back. And they did it half or two. They got so that it was annoying to you, really. When you wanted to think, you know, to have somebody walking back and forth and back and forth. So they didn't believe in any of that. And of course, they've had trouble with Annapolis and West Point, haven't they? Both, both lately.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I started out going to a college in the east. And then I came out here.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Where did you go?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I was to school in Michigan at Wayne State University.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, I didn't know that. But some of the New England schools are private schools. And I know the girls go to those and enjoy them a lot.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It seems...

speaker: John Cushman
words: I don't know about the social part of it at all. But I know they're trained in politics and things like that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I know in...

speaker: John Cushman
words: Where is Wayne State?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It's in Detroit.

speaker: John Cushman
words: It's in Detroit.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: So it's right in the city. Of course, there's a lot of theater and a lot of cultural events happening there.

speaker: John Cushman
words: I think one of my friends here in biology went back there, perhaps. He went to a Catholic school. He was a Catholic. He had one of these little bikes that you ride on with a little seat, kind of a basket on the side. And I used to go riding with him a lot in that little...

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Yeah. But it seemed that... Oh, I know in the discussion of drama back in the east, it was a lot broader. People could draw from a lot different sources than they could out in the west.

speaker: John Cushman
words: I'm trying to think of what play it was I was doing. And I asked Dr. Matkowski, that was his name. He could play the pipe organ. And so he played... But you go to Aden. And so I used that. And it gave a glorious effect. But the German woman here, oh, she thought I was awful to copy Faust in this play I was doing. I'm trying to think what I was doing. I can't seem to think. I don't think it was Bergen. It might have been. It was some other play. But it was Faust that I used it. And she couldn't stand it. She'd think I'd copy it.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Was it harder to teach the classics, do you think, in the west than it was in the east?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I never thought so. I always enjoyed teaching. I never had anyone using any dirty words or writing anything on the board like that. I never had that problem. I never had the problem of discipline.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Were you taught here between 1919 and 1930?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I taught until 1961.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Oh, I'm sorry, until 1961. Then you must have seen a lot of changes in the students. Oh, yes. And a lot of changes in attitude.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, I suppose I did. But I didn't stay long enough to get any of the rebellious part that came after my time.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: You must have also gone through so many types of drama, from Bernard Shaw to what they were doing in the 50s. Was it... you still kept up to teach those things?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I did those because every year I had the course, you see, in drama. And I'd usually reread my plays. So they would be fresh.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did you find it hard when you were trying to direct a play, going from the different styles that were materializing?

speaker: John Cushman
words: The hardest thing I had was stopping smoking. It used to make me smoke. I was so nervous. It was just nerve-wracking. We got quite a little reputation for our reading plays, too. I still think that's good. And the audiences seemed to like it, too.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Was there much theater being done by the small rural areas, or was it mostly what you were taking out to the small towns?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, I don't know. I didn't care a hoop about the school of education. There was quite a lot of antagonism there. The people who were trained in elocution, you know, in the early years, they sounded rather artificial or something. I was involved entirely with the natural, always. I started in as a kid, just a few years old. I was always reciting in Sunday school, reciting pieces, you know, until I was about 12. And then for some reason I couldn't bear to do it. But I was naturally meant to do something with plays. I should have gone ahead, perhaps, when I came out here in 1919 in New York. I did interview one of the men who taught it and read for him. I'd been doing a lot of drama guild, a lot of the plays then we'd been reading.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What kind of things were you doing on the campus when the Depression struck? Was that, did that have that many students from around here?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I didn't. It struck the faculty, of course. I remember being cut off $600 one year. When I started teaching at Syracuse, I was paid $900. That was a year's salary. And then by the time I left there, I was getting $1,600. And that included working in summer school and night school. So I worked pretty hard. And I came out here for $1,800. So you see, it was better. You would ask me why I came out here. That was the main reason, of course. I just kind of hated to go to New York and gamble that amount because I didn't have any money to help me. When I went abroad the year I graduated, my grandmother had died. And she left me my mother's share because she had died when I was young. And so I went abroad on my grandmother's money. And my mother had been born in Scotland. So I got to see some of the family. And then I had five years at Syracuse. I just had two jobs in my life. Five years at Syracuse and then 61 here. That's quite a time.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It sure is. So many changes in education that you must have been through. The different approaches that have come up.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I went to a country high school. So it wasn't difficult for me to adjust to a simple scheme as they had here. And it's been such a decent place, always. Well, Detroit wasn't like that, was it?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Oh, it was awfully dirty and awfully big.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, it was.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And not very safe.

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I suppose it would be hard. We didn't know anything about murders when I was in school. I'd come home late at night and find a night watchman welcoming me at the main gates before I came in. He let me in. And that's the way we came in. I'd go to a play and then I'd stop at one of those little restaurants, eat a piece of pie and a hunk of ice cream. Then walk up the hill, which was like a mountain, about half a mile. And get to bed about 12 o'clock. We had three theaters. We had the Keith Home Theater in Providence. And in the summer, they had the lovely stock companies. And I saw any number of plays. They were famous during the winter, you know, in New York. Of course, they weren't so long running because they traveled all over the country. I regret all the aspects of the theater that have deteriorated.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What types of things do you think have deteriorated in the theater?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I think the decency in the language they use. I didn't see the play the other night because I didn't want to see the story of Christ done with that kind of music. Jazzy music. I didn't think I'd like it. There were two or three of them, you know, that were written about the same time. And I don't know which is which. So I didn't go to that one.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Do you go and see many plays on campus?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I don't see very many because I've had a stroke and I can't walk well.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I see.

speaker: John Cushman
words: So it's very hard for me to do that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It seems like nowadays, plays on campus, now they've got that new performing arts center.

speaker: John Cushman
words: I've never seen it.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Well, they're going to start building phase two pretty soon. It's going to be all classrooms. And someday the U-Haul won't be the drama department anymore. And of course, when I came here, that's where all the plays were done and over in the education building.

speaker: John Cushman
words: You know, around Christmas time, I would be having a series of plays. The president always came. But it's so muddy up there then. None of it was paved. Nowadays, it's all paved. And you couldn't get your audience in at the time because it was so bad. I don't know how people managed it. We used to have awfully hard winters. But these last winters that you shared haven't been so bad, have they? No, no. Not much snow.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It's been bad in the east. Yes. Awfully bad in the east. Yes. So we're going to be all warm here. We won't have much water.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I enjoyed Syracuse, too. I'm sure I wouldn't like it now. And around Boston, I don't suppose I'd like it. I used to walk from my boarding place in Harvard, in Cambridge, down to the river and across the river to the Elizabeth Peabody House. Which was a settlement house, chiefly Jewish people. And they were about my best actors, too. I tell you, they were 18 or 20. They were called the Julius Caesar Tribe. I had a loving cup, you know, that they gave me, all engraved with Julius Caesar. They had done Julius Caesar. And they did for me Strife by Galsworthy. And I used to take them up to Boston Commons to listen to the rabble-rousers that would gather on those places. And they do in London, too, you know, in Hyde Park. And soapbox orators. Well, there's one actor that's connected with Michigan. I hope I can think of his name. There are two, really. But what is that first one called? He was back before 1920, chiefly. And he died. And he was quite famous as a writer. What is his name? I can't think of any play of his now.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I know Arthur Miller was there. That was his school. Arthur Miller?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, Arthur Miller's a modern one. Yes. But this other one, geez, funny, I can't think. I naturally spiel off when I have him in class. And he... I can't seem to think of the title of any of those anymore. That's one thing you'll lose when you get old, is your memory.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did you have a favorite playwright at all? One that you liked the best of all?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I think James M. Barry I liked the best.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Are there any particular reasons why?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, he's very gentle and very witty. He's a journalist. He was a very wealthy man, too. A Scotchman. That'd be one reason. When I was 15, my uncle invited me to come down to Augusta, Maine, because he was a senator. And so he invited me down. And while I was down there, I saw a New York City play that came to Augusta with a leading lady called Mary Shaw. It was her name. And she was the lead in this play. She's the only one I'd ever heard of, of course. But the wit was tremendous. It was wonderful. I've told you, though, that I'm surprised to discover that some of my early preferences seem awfully simple now. And that's true of the novels, too. I don't care a hoop about them anymore. We don't have many problems, of course, of social importance. We didn't then. Jane Austen never did that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Seems like O'Neill was the one that started to do that.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, O'Neill is pretty good, yes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: He seemed really the voice of social consciousness.

speaker: John Cushman
words: He's pretty good. He went with Professor Baker's workshop, you know. He learned that way.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did you ever happen to know him when you were there?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I never did. He wasn't there in my time. I came there later than he did. I think his shows were running when I saw plays in New York.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Seems to me he was part of the Provincetown Players.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, he was.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did you ever happen to go?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I never happened to go to Provincetown. The nearest I came was Moby Dick. Have you read Moby Dick? Yeah. You know, that's Provincetown. And then, of course, I know about Gertrude Lawrence. She had a lot to do with those summer plays. I'll tell you one that I had to do with. I was born in Skowhegan, Maine, and later went to this little country town. And in Skowhegan, they have a summer theater at a lake outside the town about half a dozen miles. It was on a streetcar. And part of the treat of going was to ride in the streetcar. And I had that half a dozen mile ride out there. And it had a very charming theater. When I first saw it, it just had trees. And just the stage had a roof on it. And they had plays a week all summer long. And one of the plays I have found useful, it had a girl in it who didn't marry the man that wanted to marry her. And so they became very old. And in the last act, you saw the two of them as old people. And her name was Gina Dare. Have you ever heard of her? Well, Gina Dare became one of those old ladies who would poison men. Do you remember that play?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Oh, Arsenic and Old Lace.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, Arsenic and Old Lace. She was one of the original actresses in that. She was a very beautiful girl when I knew her first. A young girl. And she was in this play by Gilbert, Gildan Sullen. It was a little one-act play that they were doing because it was the last show of the season. And they wanted some short ones. And so some man who could do old men's parts well did that. And I remember that. And then some of the later ones I saw, some seasons, they had nothing but O'Neil. And the time I saw that was Anna Christie. I saw a New York actress do Anna Christie. And they were doing a whole season then, but I was only over there at that time. So I did see that summer theater. And it was quite famous too. Lakewood they called it. Lakewood. And that's still running too. And then, do you know Mrs. Short? Here in college? She's a piano teacher. She had a sister in Maine who is connected with a group of people who do plays each year. She isn't connected with the plays. She does more with the business. But she's very much interested in this group. And they do Chief Lee Shakespeare up there. But they can count on those village places. They raise potatoes too. I've spent my whole life in two states that raise potatoes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Have you gotten back to the East very often?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, not very often. My father's been gone quite a while. My youngest cousin, she was nine years younger than I, died last year. I would have no reason for going. My son lives in Minneapolis. And they see wonderful shows in Minneapolis. They have a theater there. And the girls, the oldest one is 13. They play the French horn and break their arms with skis. They swim. Their father takes them fishing because he has only four girls. But I think he's bringing them up right.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I wanted to know, when you came out here the first time on the train, how long did it take you to come back?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I can't remember. Several days. Pardon me. Perhaps that's the Mississippi Department. The first one they had. They didn't ever have one. When I came here, I came here as an English professor. And then, oh, I would say about six years after I came, I was appointed head of that. And I had some assistance then. Not the assistance that Mr. Chavez gave by scenery or anything like that. But usually someone to coach the one-act plays. And I didn't do so much of that. And then we had several young assistants that didn't stay. Mr. Chavez has stayed about as long as anyone. I think perhaps the one who is here now has stayed about as long as he has. What is his name?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Mr. Sears?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes. Mr. Sears. And I liked him very much. What I've talked with him, he seemed more like what I think, anyway. I kept thinking I must make a date with him, get to talk with him about some of his plays.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: When did Miss Collette come on as the daughter?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, let's see. She came first as an undergraduate, of course. She was an English major, so I naturally had her. And she used to do funny parts. And she was here when Mr. Jennings was here, though, in the twenties.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: As a student?

speaker: John Cushman
words: As a student. Mr. Jennings didn't finish his work here when the First World War came on. So he'd been here before I came here. I didn't know him until after he was married and living in Boise. And then he came up after a year or two thinking that perhaps he would write some novels. That he could do that. And I think he could have. He didn't, but I think he could. And so I was busy having him do, write plays then. And we did pretty well. It's pretty hard in a small school, to get a big pass in that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: There was a lot of playwriting being done on campus.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Is there now?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Well, was there at your time? I don't believe so.

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, no, no. There wasn't until I started it.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I see.

speaker: John Cushman
words: And I did it in connection with my lecture course.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I'm not aware of them teaching a class like playwriting at all. Creative writing they teach.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, they had a wild-eyed man here as head of the department when I stopped. I was rather sorry about that. But he didn't approve of some of my courses. So they stopped when I stopped. And so they never did come around again, I suppose. I suppose it's more scholarly, which I think a modern university should be. But I didn't seem to need it when I was here. I probably wouldn't have stayed.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Were you the person responsible for starting the summer theater here at the university?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, no. It was Mr. Slalas, who would be in Mrs. Chavez's place. And he went to Caldwell. And he's already retired from there. And his wife was from Massachusetts. And she was an actress. They were both delightful people.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I didn't catch the name. I'm sorry.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Slalas. S-O-L-L-E-R-S. Now, his father had something to do with the theater in Washington, D.C., in connection with Abraham Lincoln, the one where he was shot to death. And that's where he came from. And he did his training at Pittsburgh. And he was a very good man. And I wrote several recommendations for him. He was in... Where did Edna Ferber live? In what town? In Michigan, I think.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Adrian, Michigan?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, it was a town where one of their private colleges is. Because that's where Mr. Slalas was.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: There's one in Adrian?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No. Well, it might have been Adrian. That wasn't the name of the college. Brown University got their college, their president from him, one of our best ones. Came from that college in Michigan. I took a group of students around the state, and I acted with them. And many of these people turned into judges, went along. And we went around. We played in Walla Walla, and we played in Boise, and of course Napa and Colorado and all those places. Weezer, Payette, and Boise. And all over the state, in fact. When Fourth of July came, we had to open a date. And we were kind of hired up. So we got a job doing a play. And we did it in the Mormon church. And I was afraid it might be questionable, but it seemed as if they enjoyed plays. And all sorts of farmers' groups, families came to this little place. It wasn't a town. It was just a sort of a little country center. And they gathered after their picnic dinner in the church. And we had the show. And my part, I'm a very innocent young man. And the play is about the wife who selects her successor. She thinks she's going to die. So she selects her successor to be my next wife. And that's what the main plot is. And he gets innocently drunk. And you'd think the Mormons wouldn't like that very much. And so that was what I had to do every night. We called ourselves the Varsity Players.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: The Varsity Players. Was it from the university? Yes. Was there any pay in that at all?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I did all the paying that was done. We didn't have any money at all. And we got by pretty well. Our big show was at Spokane. And they complimented us that it went so smoothly. And we did that two years. And we went up at Lakes. And we went up to the Montana schools. We came home that way. And Idaho Falls. So we made a circle around, you see. And we did that for two years. I always felt the need of getting out, you see. Getting out where the people were. I suppose some of them I know because of the pageant that we did in Boise. Or they play. Or else someone, someone of the students who lives in one of those towns.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Is there a script of that pageant at the university, do you know?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Mr. Jennings? Yes. Everybody just sort of...

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, I'm sure there is. I knew it until I was a little boy. This last March when we moved my home out here. I knew about all those things so I could have shown you them. But I can't now because we packed things away in storage. And that prop copy that we have, that's up there now. I left most of my books, my plays and things like that that we used to read with the library up there too. So that's... Isn't that Michigan? Zona Gayle?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I don't know. Not that I know of.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, it's about neighbors. As the title is. And you can do it when you don't have any men. You know, in a class in drama, you usually have a lot more women than men. And so it's very useful to have plays that are like that. That are good.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: There's a lot of plays I'm sure that you did that were popular in your time.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, that are gone, gone, gone. Yes. They were paperbacks. Yes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And also our perspective has changed so much.

speaker: John Cushman
words: We wanted the students, of course, taking the course, if they were interested in teaching, to have a list of plays that they could use when they went on a job. They wanted them.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: When you were teaching here, were you interested in seeing your students go on and being like professional actors? Or were you advocating that they go and teach?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I didn't. No, no, I didn't. Particularly. I don't know if they ever analyzed that I was interested in making a living, of course. And I enjoyed what the next play was going to be. And Mr. J. And it started in Montreal. And then about the Wayfaring Men. That's what the name of the play was. And that's in the library, I'm sure, Wayfaring Men. And then they moved out into the West, through Canada. And oh, down in such places as that town you mentioned. Where was it? Where you went to school?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: In Detroit. Detroit.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Detroit would be one of those French towns. And then out here, in Paris, of course. That's Idaho. They came down these streams out West here. The French fathers, see? And they were kind of like scouts, you know. And a lot of them were Indians. So that kind of life got into Idaho. But I don't know how much of it got into Troy, Idaho. Or Kendrick or Juliet. I don't know that. Or Genesee. Lots of our students have been in Genesee teaching. I don't know. I think it's hard, don't you, to evaluate what a play is going to do for you.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: You mean before you see it done? Or just reading it?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I mean doing it. Acting in it. It's the art that disappears the quickest. You see, you don't know what Maud Adams was like. I do, because I used to see her. And Helen Hayes. She's like Helen Hayes, of course. But you can't tell, as you can with music, for instance. You can get a record's reputation of piano music and give a person a pretty good idea.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It doesn't seem like we have any stars of the stage anymore.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Doesn't seem so, does it? Because all the great ones have pretty well stopped.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And there's not even... The thing that I find difficult about Moscow is there's not really a place outside of the university that you can see plays being done. You have to go into California or into a state which has a bigger city, or go up to Spokane. And that's a shame. I think being a drama student, it's important to see...

speaker: John Cushman
words: I don't get to see them anymore as I used to over in Seattle. I used to see the Repertory Theater. It's getting better every year, so they tell me. They choose plays there that they want the high school students to know. So you'll always see Macbeth or some play like that. And then they do some modern ones they've done in New York in the last year or two. And they have another theater there where they do just modern things. Very modern and generally disagreeable. And they run those all the time too. But we're living out in the country, you see, and I can't drive my car anymore. And Mrs. Cushman doesn't like to very much, so we don't do that. You have to get down to the ferry by 11 o'clock or you're likely to miss the last boat for a long time, so about 1 o'clock. And it isn't much fun to hang around the wharfs, you know.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I imagine it'd be pretty rough.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, it is. We have occasionally planned it so we'll go early in the morning over to Idaho, stay in a small town. But it's very nice. It's very nice. Everybody's very kind to the old people out here. Of course, the most prosperous part is the part where the sick people live, down at the other end. We don't see them much. They eat before we do. And many of them are in bed, of course, and many of them are in wheelchairs. They have a lot of arthritis that they're contending with. There are many more women than men. The men don't survive as long as the women do. So we have all kinds of entertainment out here. Now, tomorrow night we're having a movie, Ruggles of Red Gap. That was a very amusing movie years ago with Charles Lawton. And so we're going to have one tomorrow night.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Have you ever thought of putting together dramatic reading for all these people?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I can't because since I've had my stroke and my voice drags after a little, you have to be very stable to do that well, successfully. My eyes aren't good either. And you really have to see ahead quick.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Or be able to memorize very well.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I don't try to memorize, no. No, I can't do that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: You know, what you were saying about when you were directing plays and rehearsals in the long hours, it hasn't changed. No. We still go from 8 in the morning until 10 at night and still have to do your studies.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, you do. And I had always had to do that because I taught Chaucer and Shakespeare. I had five courses and great books, that's three. And then the modern drama, four. And what was the other one I taught?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Novels?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I did that earlier. Mr. Banks did that for me later on. Mr. Sherman, did you know him? I... He's one of the later ones. He was a student of mine. He was a very good student too. And a very good teacher.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Seems like a lot of people that came here to go to school wound up as teachers at the university. Is that usual, do you think?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, I guess it is. I don't know how many colleges take their own students. What they do at Harvard is to usually send them away for a dozen years and then bring them back when they've made good in some other school. You know, a lot of the Harvard teachers in politics land down in Washington. There's that wonderful woman who wrote a book on Johnson. I can't think of a name, but it's a brilliant book.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Yeah. I suppose. I would think that people might have the desire to go someplace.

speaker: John Cushman
words: They do one thing better than they used to. I could hardly ever get my dean to hire over one. Strangely enough, he had been a school superintendent and I imagine, thought that if you're a woman teacher, you're probably a high school teacher. And so, I used to have a lot of trouble with that. But I didn't have the trouble with the women. I think some of the men who come here though in college, you see, in English, we have practically everyone who comes here in their first year, freshman English. And so, some of them would have to have women. And I imagine some of the engineers might not want any women. Or foresters. They somehow think that they don't know enough about something. And some of our men are much better at teaching men students than they are women. We found that true.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Do you think that students related better to men on the whole?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Do you know Mrs. Boas?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: No, I've heard of her.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes. Well, she did very well with both the business school and the engineering school. Those men teachers. She was very good. She was one of my students.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Do you think they tried to keep women out of this university pretty much?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I was going to say now it's different, isn't it? Because they're paying them just the same and they're giving them good chances. The head of PE, what is her name? She lives out there on the mountain. Miss Wolf? No. She is one of the teachers in that department. But the head of the department is from Washington. She lives up there, in that hill. I can't think of a name. And then there's Dr. Stevenson. She's a very bright woman who teaches language. And they have several. The one in chemistry is supposed to be very bright. And Mrs. Shorter is very bright too. So they have plenty of good women. Do you know Miss, that piano teacher? Miss Frickman? She's very good too.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: So it was harder for women to get hired as teachers?

speaker: John Cushman
words: They're better off now.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Were women paid the same as men?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, they weren't. They weren't until recently.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: About how much less would you say a woman would get?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I don't know. You see, I don't know now what they're paid. I don't have anything to do with it. I get my pay as pension from Boise. And we don't have anything to do with this university at all.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Were they allowing, in the early part of your career teaching here, were they allowing married students to come to school here? Were they allowing them to live? Yes. Do you know, was it very strict trying to keep...

speaker: John Cushman
words: I don't know that they were. I don't know that they had any problem of that kind. I know they had plenty of homes that were meant for couples. And children too.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Were they very strict in keeping the single men and women in their own living quarters?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I don't know much about it. I didn't know anything about it.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It sounds like Dean French kept a pretty tight rein.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh yes, she was very strict. She used to be entertained at dinner by the men's fraternities. And she would lecture to them on the table manners. But you know, you wouldn't find anyone in Seattle, in the University of Washington, would be doing that probably. We've had some of our students though, as Dean, over there at Washington. I've had a student who's been over there. But Miss French, I liked her very much. I didn't mind her strictness at all.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did she go to school here?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I suppose not. I suppose she went either probably to Lewiston or one of the normal schools. She may have gone somewhere, some other state, I don't know.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: She seems very proper. She seemed very concerned with etiquette and teaching the students what was proper.

speaker: John Cushman
words: I would think that would be Catholic more than anything. I would think so.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: She seems like she was quite a lady in all sense of the word.

speaker: John Cushman
words: She, I think, was one of the strongest women deans in any of the schools here. They had several of them, women, while she was here. She was here a long time. She was related by friendship to the Jerry Days. And they, you remember, had a lot of money. And I suppose that had something to do with her prosperity here.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: This wasn't a very old university when you came to teach here.

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, it's about a year older than I am. It started about a year before I did. My secretary's mother was one of the early students here. She's a nice little old lady up in Spokane. She used to be an English teacher down in Boise High School. And she was particularly interested in drama and speech and things like that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did you find that you lacked for books and teaching materials as opposed to that?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I don't think so. In great books, that was the only problem. I was permitted to soak them each fifty cents. And then I could buy the books, you see. And we bought twenty-five copies of each book. And so those people did with twenty-five copies on reserve. And we did that all the time I taught. I taught from about twenty-five to... Well, until I stopped, of course, sixty-one. So that's a long time, twenty-five to sixty-one.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Do you remember, I'm sure you do, the influence at all? You were here when Lindley was president? Yes. When Oppen was president?

speaker: John Cushman
words: I was here when both Lindley and Oppen were president.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And then there must have been someone after them that was president when you were here?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh yes, Kelly is the next one. And then... What is the next one's name? His wife went blind in Minnesota where he went. Can't think of his name. Can you tell me?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It's not Theophilus, is it?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, no. It was before him. The man before him. I can't think of his name. I remember when he came back. I was one of those who called in to shake his hand.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Was there much difference in the way each of those men approached?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh yes. Lindley was here only one year before he went. He had been here two years when I came here. And then Dr. Oppen was the best one. I think. And he was here about eight years. He was just the most charming. He was an English professor. I naturally appreciate that. And his wife was charming too. They were lovely.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: So was there a lot of difference when you had a president that was in English as opposed to somebody that was in agriculture?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, because I got along with Dr. Kelly very well. He was in education. What is the next man's name? He's an education professor too. I can't think what his name was. He's a very good looking... Neil. He was our president for several years. Neil. They had little slivers in the wooden sidewalks.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Was that here in this town?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh yes. And then I was very fortunate because the second year we started the university club. That was the unmarried professors. And I was the only one. And so we got acquainted with each other which we never had before or would have done at any later time either. But it was very pleasant. And we had a nice cook. She was a Swedish lady. She just did a wonderful job. She looked after a dog for me. And she kept him at night in her porch which he had to sleep on. And the dog slept there. I had to let him go and live in payette. In later years because he knocked down the only policeman in town. He'd run into them. So I had to send him down on the train. One of the boys who waited on table at our house lived down there and he took him. I hope he was good to him.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did you know Dr. Church from the history department at all?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, I knew him very well. He and I used to go back east together. We'd go back to Montreal and he'd go down to New York State.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Is that where he was from?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, he lived in Pennsylvania. And I had many students from Pennsylvania from where he lived. Shortly after his death, he was buried in his home cemetery. And they had a big flood, the river. And it washed any number of bodies out of their graves. And we hope that he was kept in his place.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did you ever call on him when he lived on Adams Street?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, I didn't very often but I did sometimes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I understand.

speaker: John Cushman
words: I remember once his maiden sister was here when our little boy was three or four years old. And we took him to call him on him. So I knew him very well.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: He taught history here?

speaker: John Cushman
words: He went to school in Cornell. That's right close to Syracuse where I taught. And he knew a lot of people there. Whom I had known as teachers.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And do you suppose he came out here to teach for the same reason that you did?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, I wouldn't know. He took Professor Hume's place. Professor Hume was educated there too. And I think that's why they got him. Because Hume had had that education. He was European history.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: He's also the man that's responsible for giving us that house for the museum now.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, because he lived there. He bought it there first. And then he bought it. And he willed it to his nephew and niece. And then it came finally as a museum.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Yes, I'm very glad to have him. I understand he lived with the Adairs when they were there. He lived with the Adair family? Did you know Dr. Adair?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, I knew him. I used to run around with his daughter. One of his daughters. He had about four I think.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Ione and Bernadine?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, it was Bernadine. The singer. She used to help me with plays too. Oh really? Oh yes. And she was very much interested when we did a play in New York. And in Spokane.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: How would she help? She would help with the singing?

speaker: John Cushman
