words: Well, yes. Or if there was any problem about costuming or anything like that. I don't know if I'd want this to be reported if you turn it off. In the first play that we're here? No. I did at one time have a woman in town, a Mrs. Ann Curvis, who sewed beautifully. And she could cut anything out without a pattern. And so she made a great deal for me. And David Storr did a lot of draping of stages and things like that. Mr. Walton when he was alive. And it was remarkable how I got help from all kinds of people. But that wasn't education of course. I wasn't teaching any student anything. But that's the best I could do with what I had to work with. If I had a richer university, I could have hired a costumer who was used to it.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: So you felt like it was a lot of things you had to make do with what you had?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, I suppose we did. I sometimes used just draperies, you see. Not even windows or doors.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Could you give me an estimate about how much money you might have in a year to work for a drama production?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well finally, when Mr. Jennings came here, he was the student body president. And so he advised me to tie in with them. So I tied in with the SUI most of the time. And I'd get two or three hundred dollars a year from them.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: I see.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Of course I had to pay for my royalties as well as these other things.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: That was a long association, the drama department and the ASUI.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, yes it was.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It's only just ended.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, I knew a lot of student body presidents.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Were there ever any student body of the ASUI? Would you ever go in conflict with them at all about how much money you were spending?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, I never happened to.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: They were pretty supportive then?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, they generally did it. I didn't have to protest at all.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Were there ever doing plays that the townspeople could come and join in and be half-hearts with?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Well, those that I read, you see, for four years down at the Episcopalian Church. The townspeople were welcome to come any time. They wanted to.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: But no memorized plays?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, we didn't do that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: No community theater like we have now?

speaker: John Cushman
words: It was chiefly patronized by faculty. Hardly any students came. I don't see why. Because we had quite a lot of faculty and some of them were very good. We read plays they might have liked, as they would later on in movies. They were more or less that caliber of play.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: So you're saying you did these like readers' plays for four years? Yes. What years were you doing them in?

speaker: John Cushman
words: See, I must have started by 1920.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What years did you do the readers' drama?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, about 1922 to 1924. And then when Mr. Buchanan became president, well before then, because he was in the plays. But he wasn't president then.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: He wasn't president until about 1960.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Is it 440, though? It was when Fred Blanchard was there. That was my predecessor in coaching plays.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Who? Fred? Fred. I thought he came after you.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Oh, that's true.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Fred Blanchard followed you.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, that's true.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Because I knew Fred, he was in school and I wasn't.

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, he came after I did.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And he was in English?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, he was in drama.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And then it became Miss Collette?

speaker: John Cushman
words: Yes, Miss Collette became his assistant. I think that's the way it worked. And that's how she came in.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: You, Fred, Gene, and Chavez. Is that the way it went?

speaker: John Cushman
words: No, no. Don't you remember the one who was at Miami? He came as one of Gene's assistants.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: But he wasn't head of the drama department? No, no.

speaker: John Cushman
words: But he was one of the assistants. Yes.
